payload.text: Tarrant's boatyard builds one clinker skiff each year. This year's boat, the Wren, is planked in larch and will be launched on the first of May.
payload.title: Tarrant's boatyard

payload.text: Wick and Sons sell rope, tar and paraffin from a shed on Pier Lane. Hamish Wick opens it at dawn and shuts it once the evening ferry is in.
payload.title: Wick and Sons

payload.text: Every Thursday the market sells the week's catch of hake and ling. Bidding opens at six, and the auctioneer, Col Durrant, never takes a bid after seven.
payload.title: The Thursday auction

payload.text: Whenever fog rolls in, the horn on Gannet Rock sounds two long blasts every ninety seconds. Fishermen call it the Widow, for its mournful note.
payload.title: The fog horn

payload.text: Odran Feck has served as harbourmaster for twenty-two years. He keeps the tide tables in a green ledger and signs every mooring permit in red ink.
payload.title: The harbourmaster

payload.text: Harlow Light stands at the end of the north mole in Skerrow. Its keeper is Ines Calloway, who has trimmed the lamp every night since the winter of 1987.
payload.title: Harlow Light

payload.text: Behind the herring sheds stands a stone ice house built in 1868. Until refrigeration came, it held ice cut from Loch Brannan every February.
payload.title: The ice house

payload.text: Kelp is cut from the western reefs each spring. Dried on the shingle, it is sold by the cartload to a glassworks at Tarn Ford.
payload.title: Kelp

payload.text: Volunteers crew the lifeboat Grace Ellery from the station beside the west slip. When a vessel is reported in distress, a maroon is fired from the station roof.
payload.title: The lifeboat

payload.text: Visiting yachts pay four shillings a night to lie alongside the inner wall. The fees are collected at dusk by the harbourmaster's son, Tobin.
payload.title: Mooring fees

payload.text: Upstairs in the net loft, Bridie Moran mends drift nets by lamplight. She charges a penny a fathom and will not work on a Sunday.
payload.title: The net loft

payload.text: Pilots meet incoming ships off Gannet Rock in the cutter Sable. Her crew of four is led by Maren Ashby, the only pilot licensed for night work.
payload.title: The pilot cutter

payload.text: Mail reaches the island on the post boat Kittiwake. She calls at the west steps on Tuesdays and Fridays, weather permitting.
payload.title: The post boat

payload.text: Ferries for Quillan leave from the east slip twice a day. The first sails at 7:40 and the last at 16:15; on Sundays only the late boat runs.
payload.title: Ferries to Quillan

payload.text: The Skerrow regatta is sailed on the last Saturday of July. Its silver trophy, the Brennock Cup, was won last year by the yawl Petrel.
payload.title: The regatta

payload.text: Grey seals haul out on the Skerries each October. Children from the island school counted one hundred and twelve pups last autumn.
payload.title: The seal count

payload.text: During the great storm of 1953 the breakwater lost forty yards of stone. It was rebuilt the next summer with granite shipped from Penhallow quarry.
payload.title: The storm of 1953

payload.text: A brass bell called Old Margery hangs above the fish market. Rung three times, she warns that the spring tide will cover the lower quay.
payload.title: Old Margery
